photometry-color-001.question: Radiometric and photometric quantities correspond one to one. Which expresses the lux (lx), the unit of the photometric quantity illuminance, in terms of other photometric units?
choices: cd/m²
lm/m²
lm/sr
photometry-color-001.explanation: Illuminance is the luminous flux incident on a surface divided by its area, so 1 lx = 1 lm/m². Its radiometric counterpart is irradiance (W/m²). cd/m² is the unit of luminance, which expresses how bright a surface looks in the viewing direction (per unit area and per unit solid angle), a different quantity from illuminance. lm/sr is the candela (cd) itself, the unit of luminous intensity, the density of luminous flux that a point source sends in a given direction. Keeping the correspondence in mind — radiant flux W ↔ luminous flux lm, radiant intensity W/sr ↔ luminous intensity cd, irradiance W/m² ↔ illuminance lx, radiance W/(m²·sr) ↔ luminance cd/m² — prevents mixing up the units.

photometry-color-002.question: For the standard photopic luminous efficiency function V(λ), which describes cone-based vision in bright surroundings, which correctly pairs the wavelength of its maximum with the maximum luminous efficacy at that wavelength (luminous flux per watt)?
choices: About 555 nm, 683 lm/W
About 507 nm, 683 lm/W
About 555 nm, about 1700 lm/W
photometry-color-002.explanation: The photopic luminous efficiency function V(λ) peaks at 1 at about 555 nm (yellow-green), and 1 W of monochromatic light at this wavelength corresponds to 683 lm. The candela, the base unit of photometry, is defined as the luminous intensity of monochromatic light at 540 THz (about 555 nm) with a radiant intensity of 1/683 W/sr. About 507 nm is the peak of the scotopic function V′(λ) for rod-based vision in dim surroundings, and the maximum scotopic luminous efficacy is about 1700 lm/W. So the pairing of 507 nm with 683 lm/W and the pairing of 555 nm with about 1700 lm/W both mix photopic and scotopic values. The Purkinje effect, in which blue-green light looks relatively brighter as it gets dark, comes from this shift of the peak.

photometry-color-003.question: Which value is closest to the luminous flux of a green laser pointer with a wavelength of 532 nm and an output of 5 mW? (Take V(532 nm) = 0.88 and the maximum luminous efficacy as 683 lm/W.)
choices: About 3.4 lm
About 0.0044 lm
About 3.0 lm
photometry-color-003.explanation: The luminous flux of monochromatic light is Φv = 683 lm/W × V(λ) × Φe. Φv = 683 × 0.88 × 5×10⁻³ ≈ 3.0 lm. About 3.4 lm forgets to multiply by V(λ), treating the light as if it were at 555 nm, and about 0.0044 lm forgets the 683 lm/W and multiplies only by the luminous efficiency. At the same 5 mW, a 650 nm red laser (V ≈ 0.107) gives about 0.37 lm, roughly one eighth of the green. This is why a green laser pointer looks far brighter than a red one of the same output. For invisible infrared or ultraviolet light, V(λ) ≈ 0, so even strong radiation has almost no luminous flux.

photometry-color-004.question: A point source emits a total luminous flux of 1000 lm uniformly in all directions. Which value is closest to its luminous intensity?
choices: About 80 cd
About 160 cd
About 320 cd
photometry-color-004.explanation: Luminous intensity is the luminous flux per unit solid angle, I = dΦ/dΩ, and the solid angle of all directions is 4π sr. For a uniform point source, I = 1000 lm / 4π sr ≈ 79.6 cd, or about 80 cd. About 160 cd divides by the hemispherical solid angle 2π sr, which applies to a source radiating uniformly into one side only. About 320 cd divides by π, confusing this with the relation M = πL between the luminous exitance and luminance of a perfectly diffusing surface. Real luminaires do not radiate uniformly, so their luminous intensity is given direction by direction in a light distribution curve. With the same luminous flux, collecting the light into a narrow range with a reflector or lens raises the luminous intensity in that direction.

photometry-color-005.question: A point source is mounted on a ceiling 2 m high, and the illuminance on the floor directly below it is 100 lx. Assuming the source's luminous intensity is the same in every direction, which value is closest to the illuminance at a point on the floor 2 m horizontally from the point directly below?
choices: About 50 lx
About 35 lx
About 71 lx
photometry-color-005.explanation: Directly below, E₀ = I/h², so the luminous intensity is I = 100 × 2² = 400 cd. The distance to the point 2 m away horizontally is r = √(2² + 2²) ≈ 2.83 m, and the angle of incidence is θ = 45°. Illuminance follows both the inverse-square law for distance and the cosine law for the angle of incidence, so E = I cosθ / r² = 400 × 0.707 / 8 ≈ 35 lx (writing it as E = E₀cos³θ gives the same result). About 50 lx uses only the inverse-square law and forgets that light striking the floor obliquely spreads over a larger area. About 71 lx multiplies only by the cosine and forgets the effect of the greater distance. In lighting design, this cos³θ falloff is one cause of nonuniform floor illuminance.

photometry-color-006.question: A perfectly diffusing (Lambertian) surface with a reflectance of 0.8 is lit with an illuminance of 500 lx. Which value is closest to the luminance of this surface?
choices: About 400 cd/m²
About 64 cd/m²
About 127 cd/m²
photometry-color-006.explanation: For a perfectly diffusing surface, the luminous exitance of the reflected light, M = ρE = 0.8 × 500 = 400 lm/m², and the luminance L are related by M = πL. So L = ρE/π = 400/π ≈ 127 cd/m². About 400 cd/m² forgets to divide by π, treating luminous exitance and luminance as the same thing. A Lambertian surface has the same luminance from every viewing direction and radiates with an intensity equal to the normal intensity times cosθ, so integrating over the hemisphere gives π rather than 2π. About 64 cd/m² wrongly divides by 2π. The luminance of white paper under office lighting is of this order, around 100 cd/m².

photometry-color-007.question: A uniformly glowing, perfectly diffusing surface is viewed from twice the distance (ignore atmospheric attenuation). Which correctly pairs the change in the surface's luminance with the change in the luminous flux entering the eye from the whole surface?
choices: The luminance drops to 1/4, and the luminous flux entering the eye also drops to 1/4
The luminance is unchanged, and the luminous flux entering the eye drops to 1/4
The luminance drops to 1/2, while the luminous flux entering the eye drops to 1/4
photometry-color-007.explanation: Luminance is luminous flux per unit area per unit solid angle; it is set by the surface and does not depend on viewing distance. At twice the distance, the solid angle subtended by the pupil at each point on the surface becomes 1/4, so the luminous flux entering the eye becomes 1/4. But the area of the image on the retina also becomes 1/4, so the retinal illuminance (light per unit area) is unchanged and the surface looks just as bright. The option in which the luminance drops to 1/4 confuses luminance with the inverse-square law for illuminance from a whole source. There is no reason for the luminance to halve either. The conservation of luminance — that the image formed by a passive optical system such as a lens cannot be brighter in luminance than the object (and equals it in the same medium without losses) — is also related to this property.

photometry-color-008.question: What is the main reason an uncorrected silicon photodiode cannot be used as is as an illuminance meter?
choices: Silicon's responsivity peaks around 900 nm and differs in shape from the luminous efficiency function V(λ), so the reading shifts with the source spectrum
The current of a silicon photodiode is proportional not to the optical power but to its square root, so it cannot measure linearly in illuminance as brightness changes
With silicon's band gap (about 1.1 eV), it has no sensitivity at all to visible light and can detect only infrared
photometry-color-008.explanation: Illuminance is irradiance weighted by the luminous efficiency function V(λ), so the spectral responsivity of an illuminance meter's sensor must be matched to V(λ). Silicon responds across the whole visible range, but its responsivity peaks around 900 nm, very different from V(λ), which peaks at 555 nm. As a result, errors become large for sources whose spectra differ from the one used for calibration — for example, an incandescent lamp rich in infrared versus a white LED. Real illuminance meters approximate V(λ) by adding a photometric correction filter such as colored glass. A photodiode's photocurrent is proportional to optical power over a wide range, and it has ample sensitivity to visible light, so the other two options are wrong.

photometry-color-009.question: Which value is closest to the wavelength at which the radiation spectrum of a blackbody with a color temperature of 3000 K peaks? (Use Wien's displacement law, λmax T = 2898 µm·K.)
choices: About 580 nm
About 9.7 µm
About 966 nm
photometry-color-009.explanation: From Wien's displacement law, λmax = 2898 / 3000 ≈ 0.966 µm, or about 966 nm, in the near infrared. Most of the radiation from an incandescent lamp at a color temperature around 3000 K is infrared, and only part of it is visible, so its luminous efficacy is low, around 15 lm/W. About 9.7 µm is off by an order of magnitude and is close to the radiation peak of objects near room temperature (about 300 K). About 580 nm is a guess based on the light looking yellow, but the peak wavelength and the apparent color do not coincide. For the Sun (about 5800 K), the peak is about 500 nm, within the visible range. As the color temperature rises, the peak moves to shorter wavelengths and the color of the light changes from red to white to bluish white.

photometry-color-010.question: The specification of a white LED light says "color temperature 5000 K". Which correctly describes what this value means?
choices: It indicates that the junction of the LED chip reaches 5000 K during operation and glows white by thermal radiation from that heat
It is the temperature of the blackbody whose color is closest to the chromaticity of the light (the correlated color temperature); the higher the value, the bluer the white
It is the temperature of the blackbody whose color is closest to the chromaticity of the light; the higher the value, the redder and warmer the white, so 5000 K is a warm, incandescent-like white
photometry-color-010.explanation: The color of sources that are not blackbody radiators, such as LEDs and fluorescent lamps, is expressed by the temperature of the closest point on the blackbody locus in a uniform chromaticity diagram (such as the CIE 1960 UCS diagram), that is, the correlated color temperature. 5000 K is a neutral, daylight-like white, bluer than the warm white of about 3000 K. The hotter a blackbody, the larger the share of short-wavelength radiation, so a higher color temperature is bluish white and a lower one is reddish and warm. The option saying that a higher value means a redder, warmer white reverses this direction. Color temperature is an index of the color of the light and has nothing to do with the temperature of the emitting device; even in operation, an LED junction is only at several tens of degrees to about 100 °C (roughly 300 to 400 K). Even at the same correlated color temperature, different spectra render the colors of objects differently (color rendering).

photometry-color-011.question: A low-pressure sodium lamp emits nearly monochromatic light near 589 nm and has a very high luminous efficacy, but the colors of objects it illuminates can hardly be distinguished. Which correctly describes the index that expresses this property?
choices: The general color rendering index Ra is very low. Ra is found from color shifts of test colors against a reference light, and values near 100 look close to the reference
The general color rendering index Ra is very high. Monochromatic light has a single wavelength and no color fringing, so object colors are reproduced accurately
The correlated color temperature is very low. The lower the color temperature, the redder the light, and color rendering always gets poorer
photometry-color-011.explanation: Color rendering expresses how close the colors of objects lit by a source look to how they look under a reference light (blackbody radiation or daylight) of the same correlated color temperature. The general color rendering index Ra averages the color shifts of eight specified test colors and is 100 when there is no shift. Under monochromatic light such as a low-pressure sodium lamp, differences in the reflection spectra of objects reduce to differences in reflectance at 589 nm alone, so only lightness can be distinguished and Ra is extremely low (the formula gives a negative value, around −40). Monochromatic light does not reproduce colors accurately. Color temperature and color rendering are also separate indices: an incandescent lamp at about 2800 K has a low color temperature but an Ra of nearly 100.

photometry-color-012.question: In the CIE 1931 XYZ color system, the tristimulus values X, Y and Z are found by multiplying the spectrum of the light by the color-matching functions x̄(λ), ȳ(λ) and z̄(λ) and integrating. Which correctly describes a property of Y?
choices: Y is the component for the amount of yellow light, and the brightness information is carried by the sum of X and Z
Y is a quantity based on a real green monochromatic primary (546.1 nm), so it can even take negative values for some light spectra
ȳ(λ) was chosen equal to the photopic luminous efficiency V(λ), so Y is proportional to photometric quantities like luminance
photometry-color-012.explanation: The XYZ system was defined by linearly transforming the RGB color-matching functions obtained with real red, green and blue primaries (which include negative values) so that all the color-matching functions are positive. In doing so, ȳ(λ) was chosen to equal V(λ), so Y carries the brightness information and is tied directly to photometric quantities, as in luminance L = 683 ∫ S(λ)ȳ(λ) dλ. The color information is expressed separately by the chromaticity coordinates x and y, which are ratios of the tristimulus values. Y does not mean "yellow". And because X, Y and Z are based on imaginary primaries, they are never negative for real light. Negative values appear in the color-matching functions of the RGB system, which uses real primaries.

photometry-color-013.question: Two lights with completely different spectral distributions can look the same color under the same viewing conditions. Which correctly pairs this phenomenon with its reason?
choices: Metamerism: the eye judges color only from the responses of three cone types, so lights with matching tristimulus values look the same color
An effect of color rendering: under a high-Ra source, the differences between colors shrink so that light of any spectrum looks the same color
Color constancy: the retina analyzes the spectrum of light in detail and cancels out differences in illumination and reflectance
photometry-color-013.explanation: Color vision is determined by the responses of three types of cones (L, M and S) with different spectral sensitivities. Because the infinite-dimensional information of a spectrum is reduced to three numbers, different spectra look the same color if their three responses (tristimulus values) are equal. This is metamerism, and it is why a display can reproduce a wide range of colors with only red, green and blue light. However, the match breaks down when the illumination or the observer changes, so fabrics that matched under shop lighting can look different outdoors. Color rendering is an index of how illumination makes object colors look; it is not a mechanism that makes different spectra the same color. Color constancy is the visual system's adaptation (in the retina and brain) that keeps object colors looking the same when the illumination changes; the eye does not analyze the spectrum in detail.

photometry-color-014.question: The tristimulus values of a certain light are X = 95.05, Y = 100.0 and Z = 108.9. Which is closest to its xy chromaticity coordinates?
photometry-color-014.explanation: Chromaticity coordinates are found by dividing by the sum of the tristimulus values. With X + Y + Z = 303.95, x = 95.05/303.95 ≈ 0.313 and y = 100.0/303.95 ≈ 0.329 (z = 1 − x − y ≈ 0.358). These are the coordinates of the white point of CIE standard daylight D65 (correlated color temperature about 6500 K), used as the white reference for displays and images. x ≈ 0.950, y ≈ 1.000 merely normalizes by Y and is not a chromaticity coordinate. y ≈ 0.358 mistakes the value of z for y. Chromaticity coordinates contain no brightness information, so fully specifying a color requires three values, Yxy: (x, y) plus Y.

photometry-color-015.question: Which statement about the CIE 1931 xy chromaticity diagram is correct?
choices: Every point inside the chromaticity diagram can be represented by monochromatic light of some wavelength
The chromaticity of a mixture of two lights lies on the straight line joining the two points, and is always exactly at the midpoint regardless of which light is stronger

The chromaticities of monochromatic light lie on a horseshoe-shaped curve (the spectral locus), and the colors that can be reproduced by mixing three lights are limited to the inside of the triangle with those three points as vertices
photometry-color-015.explanation: Tracing the chromaticity of monochromatic light as the wavelength changes gives the horseshoe-shaped spectral locus. The straight line joining its red and violet ends is the line of purples, along which lie colors such as purple and magenta that cannot be produced by monochromatic light. The chromaticity of an additive mixture of two lights lies on the straight line joining the two points, at the center of gravity weighted by the sum of each light's tristimulus values (X + Y + Z), so it is not always at the midpoint. The colors that a mixture of three sources can produce lie only within the triangle with those three points as vertices; this is a display's color gamut (sRGB, BT.2020 and so on). Most colors inside the diagram are light containing multiple wavelengths, and only colors on the curve can be produced by monochromatic light. Note also that distances on the xy chromaticity diagram are not proportional to perceived color differences.

photometry-color-016.question: The sensor head of an illuminance meter has cosine correction, often using a diffuser, so that its sensitivity is proportional to cosθ for light incident at angle θ. Which is the correct reason this correction is needed?
choices: Illuminance depends only on the source's luminous intensity and distance, not on the angle of incidence, so the correction cancels the detector's angular sensitivity differences and weights light from every direction equally
Illuminance from oblique light falls as cosθ, but a flat detector's sensitivity to oblique light falls faster because of surface reflection and the like, so uncorrected it under-reads oblique light
Oblique light is all totally reflected at the sensor surface and never arrives, so the diffuser redirects it and measures oblique light with the same strength as normally incident light
photometry-color-016.explanation: Illuminance is the luminous flux per unit area arriving on a surface; when a collimated beam arrives at angle θ from the normal, the same flux is spread over 1/cosθ times the area, so the illuminance is proportional to cosθ (the cosine law). An ideal illuminance meter must therefore add up oblique light weighted by cosθ. But at a flat detector or window, Fresnel reflection increases with angle and the housing adds shadowing, so the sensitivity falls faster than cosθ. Cosine correction compensates for this shortfall by shaping the diffuser. Weighting light from every direction equally would measure the total light converging on a point rather than the illuminance on a surface. Nor is all oblique light totally reflected.

photometry-color-017.question: An LED emits a total luminous flux of 1.0 lm uniformly within a cone of half-angle 10° and nothing in other directions. Which value is closest to the luminous intensity within the cone? A cone of half-angle θ subtends a solid angle 2π(1 − cosθ).
choices: About 2.6 cd
About 0.080 cd
About 10.5 cd
photometry-color-017.explanation: The solid angle of a cone with half-angle 10° is 2π(1 − cos10°) = 2π × 0.0152 ≈ 0.0955 sr. Luminous intensity is flux per unit solid angle, so 1.0 lm/0.0955 sr ≈ 10.5 cd. About 2.6 cd uses the full angle of 20° as the half-angle, overestimating the solid angle about fourfold. About 0.080 cd is the value if the same flux were emitted uniformly in all directions (4π sr). Concentrating the same flux into a narrow angle raises the luminous intensity, so flashlights and spotlights use lenses or reflectors to brighten the center without changing the source. Flux is the total light emitted by the source, intensity is its strength in each direction, and a lens changes only the distribution of intensity.

photometry-color-018.question: On the CIE 1931 xy chromaticity diagram, the regions of colors that cannot be told apart by eye (MacAdam ellipses) vary greatly in size with position, being large in the green and small in the blue. Which statement about this property is correct?
choices: In the CIE 1976 u′v′ chromaticity diagram, a projective transformation of XYZ, the variation in ellipse size is smaller, making chromaticity differences easier to compare as distances on the diagram

The ellipse size reflects individual differences between observers' eyes, so no transformation of the diagram's coordinates changes the position dependence, and color differences are compared using the luminance Y alone
The green region with large ellipses lies outside what displays can show, so as long as one stays inside a gamut triangle, the xy distance is directly proportional to the perceived color difference
photometry-color-018.explanation: MacAdam measured the ranges of chromaticity that cannot be distinguished around given colors and showed that on the xy diagram the ellipses vary greatly in size and orientation, those in the green being much larger than those in the blue. Distances in xy are not proportional to perceived color differences. The CIE 1976 coordinates u′ = 4X/(X + 15Y + 3Z) and v′ = 9Y/(X + 15Y + 3Z) are a projective transformation of XYZ, a uniform chromaticity diagram that reduces the spread of ellipse sizes. To represent color differences including lightness even more uniformly, color spaces such as CIELAB are used. The ellipse variation appears even in standard-observer data and is a property of the xy coordinates themselves. Even inside a gamut, xy distances are not proportional to color differences.

photometry-color-019.question: Which is the correct way to find the dominant wavelength of a color on the xy chromaticity diagram?
choices: Take the wavelength of the point on the spectral locus nearest to the color's chromaticity point; the white point is not used, so every color has exactly one dominant wavelength
Draw a line from the white point through the color's point and take the wavelength where it meets the spectral locus; if it hits the purple line, use the complementary wavelength
Take the wavelength at which the radiant power of the color's spectrum is greatest; this is determined by a spectrometer measurement alone, independent of position on the diagram
photometry-color-019.explanation: The dominant wavelength is the wavelength of the monochromatic light that, mixed additively with white, matches the color. Since a mixture's chromaticity lies on the line joining the two points, extending a line from the white point (such as D65) through the color's point to the spectral locus gives the dominant wavelength. The fractional distance from the white point is the excitation purity, 1 on the locus and 0 at the white point. Colors such as magenta, whose line hits the purple line, have no corresponding monochromatic light, so they are described by the complementary wavelength found by extending the line the other way. Taking the nearest point on the locus ignores the choice of white point and departs from the definition. The spectral peak wavelength may not correspond to the color for light of different width or shape and is a different quantity.

photometry-color-020.question: A Lambertian disk source of uniform luminance L and radius r produces an illuminance E = πL r²/(r² + d²) on a surface at distance d along its axis. If this is instead calculated with the inverse-square law for a point source, E ≈ πL r²/d², what is the approximate percentage error when d is five times the source diameter (d = 10r)?
choices: About 4%
About 10%
About 1%
photometry-color-020.explanation: The ratio of the true value to the inverse-square value is E/E_point = d²/(r² + d²) = 1/(1 + (r/d)²). For d = 10r, (r/d)² = 0.01 and the ratio is 1/1.01 ≈ 0.990, so the inverse-square law overestimates by about 1%. About 4% uses the diameter 2r instead of the radius r, giving (2r/d)² = 0.04, and about 10% forgets the square, using r/d = 0.1. This is the basis of the rule of thumb, used in illuminance measurement and calculation, that the inverse-square error is within about 1% at distances of at least five times the source size. At close range the illuminance is smaller than the inverse-square value and does not grow without limit as the source is approached, tending instead to πL.

photometry-color-021.question: Which correctly describes the difference between the scotopic luminous efficiency function V′(λ), for vision by rods in dim conditions, and the photopic function V(λ)?
choices: In scotopic vision the peak sensitivity shifts to a longer wavelength, about 600 nm, so at dusk red flowers look brighter than flowers of other colors or leaves
In scotopic vision the peak shifts to a shorter wavelength, about 507 nm, so at dusk red objects look dark and blue or green ones look bright
In scotopic vision the peak stays at 555 nm and the sensitivity simply drops overall, so the order of brightness among colors does not change
photometry-color-021.explanation: In scotopic vision rods take over from cones, and the peak of the luminous efficiency moves to about 507 nm, shorter than the photopic 555 nm (the maximum scotopic luminous efficacy is about 1700 lm/W). As a result, red and blue objects that looked equally bright in daylight appear, at dusk, with the red darker and the blue or green relatively brighter. This is called the Purkinje effect. Saying that the peak moves to longer wavelengths gets the direction backward. A sensitivity that merely drops overall cannot explain why the appearance changes with color. Because there is only one type of rod, color can hardly be distinguished in scotopic vision.

photometry-color-022.question: The effect of a color-temperature conversion filter is nearly constant, regardless of the original color temperature, when expressed as a difference in mired value M = 10⁶/T (T is the color temperature in K). Which value is closest to the change in mired value for a filter that makes 3200 K light look like 5500 K light?
choices: About +131 mired
About −2300 mired
About −131 mired
photometry-color-022.explanation: The mired value is 10⁶/3200 ≈ 312.5 at 3200 K and 10⁶/5500 ≈ 181.8 at 5500 K, so the change is 181.8 − 312.5 ≈ −131 mired. A filter that raises the color temperature (adds blue) lowers the mired value, so the change is negative. +131 mired takes the difference the wrong way round and corresponds to a filter that lowers the color temperature (adds red). −2300 mired wrongly uses the difference in color temperature itself. Expressed as a color-temperature difference, the same filter produces very different changes for low and high color temperatures, but the mired difference is nearly constant, which is why the strength of color-conversion filters for cameras and lighting is given in mireds.

photometry-color-023.question: Light A, with chromaticity (x, y) = (0.60, 0.30) and Y = 30, and light B, with (x, y) = (0.20, 0.60) and Y = 120, illuminate the same surface together (additive mixing). Which value is closest to the chromaticity of the mixture?
photometry-color-023.explanation: Chromaticity coordinates are fractions of the tristimulus sum S = X + Y + Z, so for a mixture X, Y and Z are each added and then divided again. From S = Y/y, light A has S = 30/0.30 = 100 (X = 60) and light B has S = 120/0.60 = 200 (X = 40). The mixture has X = 100, Y = 150 and S = 300, so x = 100/300 ≈ 0.33 and y = 150/300 = 0.50. (0.40, 0.45) is the simple average of the two chromaticities, and (0.28, 0.54) is the average weighted by Y. The chromaticity of a mixture lies on the straight line joining the two points, closer to the light with the larger S.

photometry-color-024.question: Why is the luminous efficacy (luminous flux per watt of electrical power) of an incandescent lamp with a color temperature of about 2800 K as low as about 15 lm/W?
choices: The filament is so hot that most of its radiation is ultraviolet, which the eye cannot see
The peak of its emission spectrum lies in the near infrared at about 1 µm, so most of the radiation is infrared, where the luminous efficiency is nearly zero
Most of its radiation is visible, but it contains a lot of yellow and is off the 555 nm peak of the luminous efficiency
photometry-color-024.explanation: By Wien's displacement law, λmax = 2898/T [µm], the emission of a 2800 K blackbody peaks in the near infrared at about 1.03 µm, and only about a tenth of the radiation falls in the visible range (380–780 nm). Most of the rest is infrared, where the luminous efficiency is almost zero, so it contributes nothing to the luminous flux and is lost as heat. At 2800 K there is very little ultraviolet; saying that most of the radiation is ultraviolet reverses the relation between temperature and wavelength. The bias of the visible light toward yellow and red lowers the efficacy slightly, but the premise that most of the radiation is visible is wrong, so it is not the main reason. LED lighting emits almost no radiation at invisible wavelengths, which allows a much higher luminous efficacy.

photometry-color-025.question: A sheet of white paper looks white both in daylight and under an incandescent lamp, even though the spectrum of the light it reflects is very different. Which correctly pairs this property with the corresponding processing in a camera?
choices: Chromatic adaptation, in which the eye adjusts the sensitivity of its three cone types to the color of the illumination; in a camera, white balance adjusts the R, G and B gains
Metamerism, in which the light from the paper has the same tristimulus values even though the two illuminant spectra differ; in a camera, gamma correction adjusts the tone scale
Color rendering, because both illuminants have a high color rendering index; in a camera, exposure compensation adjusts the amount of light reaching the sensor
photometry-color-025.explanation: The eye adjusts the sensitivity of each of its three cone types, L, M and S, to the color of the illumination, discounting the color cast of the light when it sees the color of objects. This is chromatic adaptation, and the von Kries model, which treats each cone response as a ratio to the response to the illuminant's white, is commonly used. In a camera, white balance, which adjusts the gains of the R, G and B signals so that white or gray objects are rendered neutral, plays this role. White paper under daylight and under an incandescent lamp has different tristimulus values, so this is not metamerism. The color rendering index measures how well an illuminant reproduces colors and is not the reason the paper looks white. Gamma correction and exposure compensation process brightness and cannot correct a color cast.
